description: Define who your product, service, or personal brand is NOT for, then use that exclusion to sharpen messaging for who it IS for. Specificity attracts the right people better than broadening ever does.

steps.description: List the types of people who buy but then churn, complain, or drain resources disproportionately.

inputs.name: customer-data
inputs.desc: Customer list with churn status, complaints, support tickets, and refund history

inputs.name: offering-description
inputs.desc: What you sell, do, or represent (product, service, personal brand, cause)

outputs.name: churn-complaint-patterns
outputs.desc: Recurring patterns among customers who churned, complained, or consumed disproportionate resources

outputs.name: high-cost-segments
outputs.desc: Segments that cost more to serve than they return in value

process: Pull the list of customers who churned within 90 days, or who filed more than two complaints, or who requested refunds.
For each, note what they expected, what they actually needed, and where the mismatch surfaced.
Group the patterns: wrong use case, wrong skill level, wrong budget range, wrong timeline expectations, or wrong values alignment.
Rank the groups by frequency and by cost (support time, refund dollars, team morale drain).

steps.description: Define the anti-persona: a composite profile of the person you are explicitly choosing not to serve.

inputs.name: churn-complaint-patterns
inputs.desc: Recurring mismatch patterns from the audit

inputs.name: high-cost-segments
inputs.desc: Segments that cost more than they return

outputs.name: anti-persona-profile
outputs.desc: Composite profile including demographics, behaviors, expectations, and the specific mismatch that makes them a poor fit

outputs.name: exclusion-rationale
outputs.desc: Why serving this person harms both them and you

process: From the patterns, write one composite profile. Give it a name. Describe: what they expect, what they need, how they evaluate, and what outcome they actually want.
For each trait, explain the mismatch: why your offering does not serve this need, and why trying to serve it dilutes what you do for the right people.
State the exclusion rationale in one sentence: serving this person means either changing what you are or disappointing them, and neither outcome is acceptable.

steps.description: Write a 'not for you if' statement that can appear in marketing, sales conversations, and onboarding materials.

inputs.name: anti-persona-profile
inputs.desc: Composite profile of who you are not for

inputs.name: exclusion-rationale
inputs.desc: Why serving them harms both sides

outputs.name: not-for-you-statement
outputs.desc: Plain language statement of who this is not for, written to repel the wrong buyer without being hostile

outputs.name: placement-recommendations
outputs.desc: Where to put the statement (landing page, sales script, onboarding email, FAQ)

process: Write the statement in second person: 'This is not for you if...' followed by 3-5 concrete conditions drawn from the anti-persona profile.
Test each condition: would the right customer read it and think 'that is not me'? If a condition could scare the right customer, rewrite it.
Recommend placement: the statement works hardest when it appears before the person commits time (landing page, pricing page, first sales call).
Note: this statement often increases conversion rate because it signals confidence and specificity, which the right buyer finds reassuring.

steps.description: Use the anti-persona as a contrast to sharpen the definition of who you ARE for. The exclusion reveals the inclusion.

outputs.name: sharpened-ideal-profile
outputs.desc: Refined ideal customer profile that is specific enough to recognize on sight

outputs.name: differentiating-traits
outputs.desc: The 3-5 traits that most clearly separate the ideal from the anti-persona

process: For each anti-persona trait, write the opposite: what the ideal customer expects, needs, and values instead.
Identify the 3-5 differentiating traits that most cleanly separate the ideal from the anti-persona. These are your targeting criteria.
Write the ideal profile in the same format as the anti-persona: a named composite with demographics, behaviors, expectations, and desired outcome.
Test: if you read both profiles to a salesperson, could they sort a new lead into one or the other within five questions?

steps.description: Run every piece of current messaging through the anti-persona filter. If the anti-persona would find it appealing, it is too generic.

inputs.name: differentiating-traits
inputs.desc: Traits that separate ideal from anti-persona

outputs.name: filtered-messaging
outputs.desc: Revised messaging that speaks directly to the ideal profile and would not attract the anti-persona

outputs.name: removed-generic-claims
outputs.desc: Claims, features, and benefits that were removed because they appealed equally to both profiles

process: Collect every piece of current messaging: website copy, ads, sales decks, email sequences, social bios.
For each claim or benefit, ask: would the anti-persona find this appealing? If yes, it is too generic. Flag it.
Rewrite flagged claims to speak specifically to the differentiating traits. Replace 'for everyone' language with 'for people who' language.
List what was removed. These removed items are your competitors' messaging territory, and you are choosing not to fight there.

steps.description: Measure the impact of anti-persona targeting on conversion rates, churn, and customer quality.

inputs.name: not-for-you-statement
inputs.desc: The exclusion statement placed in marketing materials

outputs.name: targeting-impact-report
outputs.desc: Before/after comparison of conversion rate, churn rate, support ticket volume, and customer satisfaction

outputs.name: refinement-recommendations
outputs.desc: Adjustments to the anti-persona or messaging based on measured results

process: Set the baseline: conversion rate, churn rate, support tickets per customer, and average customer satisfaction score before the change.
Deploy the filtered messaging and not-for-you statement. Run for at least 30 days or 100 conversions, whichever comes first.
Measure: did conversion volume drop? If yes, by how much? Did conversion quality improve (lower churn, fewer tickets, higher satisfaction)?
Calculate the net effect: fewer but better customers often produces higher revenue per customer and lower cost to serve. Show the math.

description: Study the deals, opportunities, or attempts you lost instead of the ones you won. Losers reveal the real objections, decision criteria, and failure points that winners hide.

steps.description: Build an inventory of recent losses: deals that stalled, customers who chose a competitor, attempts that failed, opportunities that went nowhere.

inputs.name: pipeline-data
inputs.desc: Sales pipeline, project history, or personal attempt log covering at least the last 6 months

inputs.name: loss-definition
inputs.desc: What counts as a loss (closed-lost deal, ghosted prospect, rejected proposal, abandoned project)

outputs.name: loss-inventory
outputs.desc: Structured list of losses with date, prospect or opportunity name, stage at which it stalled, and stated reason for loss

outputs.name: loss-volume-summary
outputs.desc: Count and percentage of losses by stage and by stated reason

process: Pull every closed-lost or abandoned opportunity from the last 6 months. Include deals that went silent (no explicit no, just disappeared).
For each loss, record: when it entered the pipeline, when it stalled, what stage it reached, and the stated reason (if one was given).
Categorize: competitor chosen, no decision made, budget cut, timing wrong, went silent, or explicit objection.
Calculate the loss rate by stage: what percentage of opportunities die at each point in the process?

steps.description: For each loss, dig beneath the stated reason to find the likely real reason. The stated reason is a social convenience. The real reason is the useful signal.

inputs.name: loss-volume-summary
inputs.desc: Loss patterns by stage and reason

outputs.name: real-reason-analysis
outputs.desc: For each loss: the stated reason, the likely real reason, the evidence for the real reason, and the moment the loss became inevitable

outputs.name: objection-map
outputs.desc: The actual objections ranked by frequency, with the language prospects used

process: For each loss, review the communication trail: emails, call notes, proposal feedback. Look for the moment energy dropped.
Common translations: 'budget' often means 'not convinced of the value'; 'timing' often means 'not urgent enough'; 'went silent' often means 'found something easier'.
For competitor losses, identify what the competitor offered that you did not (or what they communicated that you did not). The gap is the real reason.
For the losses that went silent: reconstruct the last touchpoint. What was asked of the prospect? If it was too much too soon, the ask was the real reason.

steps.description: Find the patterns across losses. The individual reasons are anecdotes. The patterns are your improvement roadmap.

outputs.name: loss-patterns
outputs.desc: The 3-5 recurring patterns that explain the majority of losses

outputs.name: pattern-stage-map
outputs.desc: Which patterns strike at which stages in the process

process: Group the real reasons into clusters. Name each cluster by the underlying failure: unclear value, wrong audience, weak follow-up, missing proof, or process friction.
For each cluster, count the losses. The largest cluster is your biggest leak.
Map each cluster to the stage where the loss typically occurs. A pattern that kills deals early is a positioning problem. A pattern that kills deals late is a trust or proof problem.
Rank the patterns by impact: number of losses times average deal value (or opportunity value). This is the roadmap priority order.

steps.description: For the top patterns, construct the counterfactual: what would have changed the outcome? This turns the analysis into specific actions.

outputs.name: counterfactual-actions
outputs.desc: For each pattern: the specific change to messaging, process, proof, or offering that would address it

outputs.name: implementation-priority
outputs.desc: Actions ranked by expected impact (losses prevented times value per loss)

process: For each pattern, pick the three most representative losses. Replay each from the failure point: what if you had said X instead of Y? Provided proof Z? Asked a different question?
Write the specific change: a new slide in the deck, a different opening question, a case study that addresses this objection, a pricing structure change, or a process simplification.
Estimate the impact: if this change prevents half the losses in this pattern, how much value does that recover?
Rank by recovered value divided by implementation effort. The highest-ratio changes go first.

steps.description: Compare the loss patterns against your wins to confirm the diagnosis. If your wins share traits that your losses lack, the contrast validates the pattern.

inputs.name: counterfactual-actions
inputs.desc: Proposed changes based on loss patterns

outputs.name: validated-patterns
outputs.desc: Loss patterns confirmed by contrast with wins

outputs.name: false-pattern-flags
outputs.desc: Patterns that appeared in losses but also appear in wins, meaning they are not the real cause

process: Pull your recent wins. For each, note the same attributes: stage progression, objections raised (and overcome), proof provided, and decision timeline.
Compare: what did the wins have that the losses lacked? Common differences: earlier proof of value, a champion inside the buyer, a triggering event that created urgency, or a simpler ask.
Flag any loss pattern that also appears in wins. If 'budget concern' appears in both wins and losses, budget is not the deciding factor. Remove it from the roadmap.
The validated patterns are the ones that appear in losses but not in wins. These are your real failure modes.

steps.description: Produce the loss analysis report: the patterns, the counterfactual actions, and the measurement plan to track whether the changes work.

outputs.name: loss-analysis-report
outputs.desc: The full report: patterns, evidence, actions, priorities, and a 90-day measurement plan

outputs.name: tracking-metrics
outputs.desc: The specific metrics to watch (loss rate by stage, objection frequency, win rate change) and the baseline values

process: Write the report in four sections: what we found (patterns), why it matters (value at stake), what to do (actions in priority order), and how to measure (metrics and timeline).
For each action, name the owner, the deadline, and the metric that moves if it works.
Set the measurement cadence: re-run this analysis quarterly. Compare the new loss patterns against the old ones. If the patterns shifted, the actions worked. If they persisted, the actions missed.

description: Mine competitor reviews (1-star to 3-star) to find exact objections, unmet needs, and the language real customers use to describe market gaps. Their complaints are your marketing copy and product roadmap.

steps.description: Identify where competitor reviews live: app stores, G2, Capterra, Trustpilot, Amazon, Yelp, Google Maps, Reddit, niche forums.

inputs.name: competitor-list
inputs.desc: The competitors to mine (products, services, or brands that your target audience also considers)

inputs.name: market-category
inputs.desc: The product or service category you compete in

outputs.name: review-source-map
outputs.desc: For each competitor: the platforms where reviews exist, approximate volume, and the date range covered

outputs.name: collection-plan
outputs.desc: Which sources to prioritize and how many reviews to collect per competitor (target: 50-100 negative reviews per competitor)

process: For each competitor, search the major review platforms. Note which platforms have the most reviews and the most detailed negative reviews.
Prioritize platforms where reviewers write paragraphs, not just stars. Detailed complaints contain the language and expectations you need.
Plan the collection: aim for 50-100 negative reviews (1-3 stars) per competitor. If a competitor has fewer than 50 negative reviews, include the 3-star reviews that contain specific complaints.

steps.description: Collect the negative reviews and structure them for analysis. Extract: what the customer expected, what they got, and how they describe the gap.

inputs.name: collection-plan
inputs.desc: How many to collect per competitor and platform

outputs.name: structured-reviews
outputs.desc: Each review broken into: competitor name, platform, star rating, what was expected, what was received, and the exact gap description in the reviewer's words

outputs.name: raw-language-bank
outputs.desc: The exact phrases and sentences customers used to describe their frustration, organized by theme

process: For each review, extract three things: (1) what the customer expected or was promised, (2) what they actually experienced, (3) how they describe the gap in their own words.
Copy the exact language. Do not paraphrase. The value is in the specific words customers choose, because those words are what other potential customers will search for and relate to.
Tag each review with the theme: missing feature, poor support, pricing mismatch, reliability problem, onboarding friction, or broken promise.

steps.description: Find the patterns across hundreds of complaints. The recurring gaps are the market opportunities. The rare complaints are noise.

inputs.name: structured-reviews
inputs.desc: Reviews broken into expectation, reality, and gap description

outputs.name: gap-pattern-report
outputs.desc: The 5-10 most common gaps ranked by frequency, with representative quotes and the number of reviews mentioning each

outputs.name: unmet-needs-list
outputs.desc: Needs that customers express but no competitor in the market currently satisfies

process: Count the frequency of each theme. The top themes are the biggest market gaps.
Within each theme, identify the specific unmet need. 'Bad support' is a theme. 'Cannot get a human within 24 hours for billing issues' is the unmet need.
Separate gaps into two categories: gaps you can fill (product/service opportunities) and gaps you cannot fill (structural limitations of the category). Focus on the first.
Rank by frequency times severity. A gap mentioned by 40% of reviewers at 1 star is more valuable than a gap mentioned by 10% at 3 stars.

steps.description: Turn the gap descriptions into marketing copy. The customers already wrote the copy for you in their complaints.

inputs.name: gap-pattern-report
inputs.desc: The common gaps with representative quotes

inputs.name: raw-language-bank
inputs.desc: Exact customer phrases organized by theme

outputs.name: derived-marketing-copy
outputs.desc: Headlines, subheads, and ad copy derived directly from customer complaint language, pre-answering the objections competitors created

outputs.name: seo-keyword-list
outputs.desc: The exact phrases customers use to describe the problem, which are also the phrases they will search for

process: For each top gap, find the 3 most vivid customer quotes. These quotes describe the pain in language that other customers will immediately recognize.
Write headlines that pre-answer the complaint: if the complaint is 'took 3 days to get a response', the headline is 'Same-day response, every time' (or whatever your actual capability is).
Extract the search-worthy phrases. Customers searching for alternatives will type the same words they use in reviews: 'alternative to X that actually Y', 'X but with Z'.
Do not fabricate claims you cannot deliver. Only write copy for gaps you actually fill. Unfilled gaps go to the product roadmap, not the marketing copy.

steps.description: Feed the unfilled gaps into product planning. These are features or improvements that real customers are asking for with their wallets when they leave competitors.

inputs.name: unmet-needs-list
inputs.desc: Needs that no competitor currently satisfies

inputs.name: gap-pattern-report
inputs.desc: All gaps ranked by frequency and severity

outputs.name: feature-opportunity-list
outputs.desc: Product or service features that would fill a proven market gap, ranked by the number of customers who expressed the need

outputs.name: competitive-moat-candidates
outputs.desc: Gaps so large and so frequently mentioned that filling them would be a lasting differentiator

process: List every gap you cannot currently fill. For each, estimate the effort to fill it (small, medium, large).
Rank by frequency times feasibility. A gap mentioned by 100 reviewers that takes medium effort to fill is a better bet than a gap mentioned by 200 that takes large effort.

Identify moat candidates: gaps that are hard to fill (requiring deep expertise, infrastructure, or a fundamentally different approach). If you fill a hard-to-fill gap, competitors cannot easily copy it.
Add the top 3-5 items to the product roadmap with the review evidence attached. The evidence makes the case for building it.

steps.description: Set the cadence for re-mining. Markets shift, competitors respond, and new complaints surface. This is not a one-time exercise.

outputs.name: refresh-schedule
outputs.desc: When and how to re-run the mining process (quarterly recommended), with triggers for ad-hoc runs

outputs.name: monitoring-setup
outputs.desc: Ongoing review monitoring alerts for new complaints that match known gap patterns or reveal new ones

process: Set a quarterly cadence: re-run the collection and analysis every 3 months. Markets move; new complaints surface as competitors ship changes.

Set ad-hoc triggers: if a competitor launches a major update, re-mine within 2 weeks to see the reaction. If you launch a feature that fills a gap, monitor competitor reviews to see if customers notice.
Set up alerts (Google Alerts, review platform notifications) for your competitors' brand names plus negative sentiment keywords.

description: Detect when a marketing or growth channel is saturating before you waste resources on declining returns. Track cost per acquisition over time, spot the inflection, and shift resources before the channel dies.

steps.description: Inventory every active growth channel and establish the baseline cost per acquisition and volume for each.

inputs.name: channel-list
inputs.desc: All active marketing and growth channels (paid ads, organic search, social, referral, email, content, partnerships, events, outbound)

inputs.name: spend-and-results-data
inputs.desc: Monthly spend and acquisition counts per channel for at least the last 6 months

outputs.name: channel-baseline-report
outputs.desc: For each channel: monthly CPA, monthly volume, CPA trend direction, and volume trend direction

outputs.name: channel-health-scores
outputs.desc: Each channel scored as growing, stable, or declining based on the CPA and volume trends

process: For each channel, calculate the monthly CPA (total spend divided by acquisitions) for each of the last 6 months.
Plot the CPA trend: rising, flat, or falling. Plot the volume trend: rising, flat, or falling.
Score each channel: falling CPA plus rising volume is healthy. Rising CPA plus flat volume is saturating. Rising CPA plus falling volume is dying.
Flag any channel where CPA rose for 3 or more consecutive months. This is the early warning signal.

steps.description: For each flagged channel, analyze whether the CPA rise is temporary (seasonal, auction fluctuation) or structural (audience exhaustion).

inputs.name: channel-baseline-report
inputs.desc: CPA and volume trends per channel

inputs.name: channel-health-scores
inputs.desc: Channels scored as growing, stable, or declining

outputs.name: saturation-diagnosis
outputs.desc: For each flagged channel: temporary vs structural, evidence for the diagnosis, and estimated remaining runway

outputs.name: addressable-audience-estimates
outputs.desc: For each saturating channel: the estimated total addressable audience, the percentage already reached, and the remaining pool

process: Check for seasonal effects: does this channel always see CPA rises in this quarter? Compare against the same period in prior years if data exists.
Check for auction competition: did a new competitor enter the auction? Did platform costs rise across all advertisers? If yes, the rise is market-wide, not saturation.

If neither seasonal nor competitive: estimate the total addressable audience in the channel. Compare against cumulative reach. If you have reached over 60% of the addressable audience, structural saturation is likely.
Estimate the remaining runway: at current CPA growth rate, when does CPA cross the profitability threshold?

steps.description: Evaluate alternative channels where resources could shift. Compare the CPA, volume ceiling, and ramp time for each alternative.

inputs.name: saturation-diagnosis
inputs.desc: Which channels are saturating and why

outputs.name: alternative-channel-comparison
outputs.desc: Each alternative channel rated on: expected CPA, volume ceiling, ramp time to reach steady state, and overlap with saturating channel's audience

outputs.name: reallocation-candidates
outputs.desc: The top 2-3 channels to shift resources into, with expected impact

process: List channels not currently active or underinvested. For each, research the typical CPA range for your category.
Estimate the volume ceiling: how many acquisitions per month can this channel realistically produce?
Estimate the ramp time: how long from first spend to steady-state CPA? Paid channels ramp in weeks. Content and SEO ramp in months. Partnerships ramp in quarters.
Check audience overlap: if the saturating channel and the alternative reach the same people, shifting budget just moves the problem.

steps.description: Plan the resource shift: how much to pull from saturating channels, how much to invest in alternatives, and how fast to make the transition.

inputs.name: saturation-diagnosis
inputs.desc: Saturating channels and their remaining runway

outputs.name: reallocation-plan
outputs.desc: Month-by-month budget shift from saturating to growing channels, with expected CPA and volume at each stage

outputs.name: risk-mitigation-steps
outputs.desc: What to do if the alternative channel underperforms during ramp-up

process: Do not cut the saturating channel to zero. Reduce spend to the point where marginal CPA equals your profitability threshold. This captures the remaining value without overpaying.
Allocate the freed budget to alternatives in proportion to their expected efficiency (lower CPA, higher ceiling first).
Plan for the ramp: new channels often underperform in the first 30-60 days. Build a bridge budget that accepts higher CPA during ramp-up.
Set the kill criteria: if an alternative channel does not reach its target CPA within 90 days, reallocate again.

steps.description: Set up ongoing monitoring so saturation is caught early next time, not after months of wasted spend.

inputs.name: channel-baseline-report
inputs.desc: Baseline CPA and volume for all channels

outputs.name: monitoring-dashboard-spec
outputs.desc: Dashboard design showing: CPA trend per channel, volume trend, saturation alerts, and reallocation triggers

outputs.name: alert-thresholds
outputs.desc: The specific thresholds that trigger a review: CPA rise of X% for Y consecutive periods, volume decline of Z%

process: Define the alert: CPA rises more than 15% month-over-month for 2 consecutive months triggers a review. Volume declines more than 20% month-over-month triggers a review.
Build the dashboard with one row per channel: current CPA, 3-month CPA trend, current volume, 3-month volume trend, health score (green/yellow/red).
Set the review cadence: monthly for all channels, weekly for any channel in yellow or red status.
Document the response playbook: when an alert fires, re-run the saturation diagnosis and alternative evaluation steps.

description: Design a referral system where the act of referring creates value for the referrer independent of conversion. Build the ask into moments of satisfaction, track referral chains, and identify super-connectors.

steps.description: Map why people refer. The motivation determines the mechanism. Social capital, financial reward, and status work differently.

inputs.name: customer-profile
inputs.desc: Who your current customers or users are (demographics, relationship to your offering, communication patterns)

inputs.name: offering-type
inputs.desc: What you offer (product, service, community, content, cause)

outputs.name: motivation-map
outputs.desc: The primary referral motivation for your audience: social capital (they look good recommending you), financial (they earn money), or status (they gain recognition)

outputs.name: referral-value-design
outputs.desc: What value the referrer receives from the act of referring, independent of whether the referral converts

process: Survey or interview 10-20 customers who have already referred someone. Ask: why did you refer? What did you get out of it? Would you refer again? What would make it easier?
Classify the motivation: social capital (personal relationships, professional reputation), financial (discount, commission, credit), or status (leaderboard, badge, early access).

Design the referral value so it accrues to the referrer immediately upon referring, not upon conversion. If the reward is contingent on the referral buying, the referrer feels like a salesperson, not a helper.

steps.description: Find the moments in the customer journey when satisfaction is highest. The referral ask should land at a peak, not at signup.

inputs.name: referral-value-design
inputs.desc: What value the referrer gets from the act

outputs.name: peak-satisfaction-moments
outputs.desc: The 3-5 moments in the customer journey when satisfaction is highest (first success, milestone reached, problem solved, compliment received)

outputs.name: ask-placement-plan
outputs.desc: Where to place the referral ask relative to each peak moment

process: Map the customer journey from first contact to longtime user. Identify the emotional peaks: first 'aha' moment, first measurable result, first time they told someone about it unprompted.
The referral ask goes immediately after the peak, not before. Asking before the peak feels premature. Asking at the peak converts because the person is already feeling generous.
Do not ask at signup. The person has not experienced value yet. Asking them to refer before they have received value is asking them to spend social capital on credit.

Test multiple placements. The optimal moment varies by product type: for consumer products, it is after first use. For services, it is after first result. For communities, it is after first meaningful interaction.

steps.description: Build the referral mechanism: how the referrer shares, what the recipient sees, and how the loop closes.

outputs.name: referral-mechanism-spec
outputs.desc: The complete referral flow: trigger, ask copy, sharing method, recipient landing experience, and reward delivery

outputs.name: friction-audit
outputs.desc: Every step in the referral flow rated by friction level, with recommendations to reduce each

process: Design the sharing method: unique link (lowest friction), email invitation (higher trust), or in-product share button (contextual). Match the method to where your customers communicate.
Write the ask copy. It should: acknowledge the peak moment, give a reason to share that benefits the referrer (not just the recipient), and make sharing require one click or less.
Design the recipient landing: when someone clicks a referral link, they should see who referred them, why, and what they get. Personal context converts better than generic landing pages.
Reduce friction at every step. Count the clicks from 'decide to refer' to 'referral received.' If it is more than 3 clicks, simplify.

steps.description: Track referral chains to find super-connectors: the small percentage of referrers who generate a disproportionate share of referrals.

outputs.name: tracking-schema
outputs.desc: Data model for tracking referral chains: who referred whom, when, whether it converted, and the chain depth

outputs.name: super-connector-criteria
outputs.desc: The threshold that defines a super-connector (top 5% by referral volume or chain depth)

process: Build the tracking: each referral link is unique to the referrer. When a referral converts, log the chain: referrer, recipient, timestamp, and whether the recipient also refers.
Calculate referral depth: how many levels deep does a chain go? A chain of 1 (direct referral) is normal. A chain of 3 or more indicates a viral loop is working.
Identify super-connectors: the people who generate 5 or more referrals, or whose referrals generate further referrals. These people are 10-50x more valuable than average customers.
Design differentiated treatment for super-connectors: early access, direct communication channel, recognition, or increased rewards. The goal is to keep them active.

steps.description: Acknowledge every referral visibly. Unacknowledged referrals kill the loop. Acknowledged referrals reinforce the behavior.

outputs.name: acknowledgment-workflow
outputs.desc: The automated and manual acknowledgment touchpoints: instant notification, reward delivery, and periodic gratitude

outputs.name: referral-loop-report
outputs.desc: Complete referral loop design document covering motivation, mechanism, tracking, and acknowledgment

process: Instant acknowledgment: the moment someone uses a referral link, notify the referrer. 'Your friend just signed up' or 'Someone used your recommendation.' This closes the feedback loop immediately.
Reward delivery: deliver the referrer's value within 24 hours. Delayed rewards feel like broken promises. If the reward is credit or status, apply it instantly.
Periodic gratitude: monthly or quarterly, send super-connectors a personal note (not automated template) thanking them. Name the impact: 'You brought in 12 people this quarter. That matters.'

Measure the loop: referral rate (what percentage of customers refer), conversion rate (what percentage of referrals convert), and loop ratio (referrals per referrer per month). A healthy loop has a referral rate above 10% and a conversion rate above 20%.

description: Position by removing claims instead of adding them. List every feature, benefit, and claim, then subtract until only the irreducible core remains. That core is your positioning. Everything else dilutes the signal.

steps.description: Inventory every claim, feature, and benefit in your current messaging across all channels.

inputs.name: current-messaging
inputs.desc: All current marketing materials: website, ads, sales decks, email sequences, social profiles, packaging

inputs.name: offering-description
inputs.desc: What you sell, do, or represent

outputs.name: claim-inventory
outputs.desc: Every distinct claim, feature, and benefit extracted from current messaging, deduplicated

outputs.name: claim-count
outputs.desc: Total number of distinct claims (most businesses have 15-40; if yours has more than 10, there is room to subtract)

process: Go through every piece of messaging. For each, extract the distinct claims: what it says you do, what benefits it promises, what features it highlights.
Deduplicate: many claims will appear in slightly different words across channels. Merge them into one canonical version.
Count them. Most businesses carry 15-40 distinct claims across their materials. The number itself is diagnostic: more than 10 usually means the positioning is blurry.

steps.description: For each claim, ask: if I removed this, would the right customer still choose me? If yes, remove it. If no, keep it.

inputs.name: claim-inventory
inputs.desc: Every distinct claim in current messaging

outputs.name: essential-claims
outputs.desc: The claims that survived the subtraction test: removing any one of them would cause the right customer to choose differently

outputs.name: removable-claims
outputs.desc: The claims that can be removed without changing the right customer's decision

process: Take each claim one at a time. Imagine your messaging without it. Ask: would the right customer (the one you defined in your ideal profile) still choose you?
If yes: the claim is not load-bearing. It is filler, table stakes, or a me-too statement. Mark it removable.
If no: the claim is essential. It is a reason the right customer chooses you over the alternative. Keep it.
Be honest about table stakes. 'Fast support' is table stakes in most categories. If every competitor also claims fast support, removing it does not change the decision.
If you cannot tell whether a claim is essential, ask 5 customers: 'If we stopped saying X, would it change your decision?' Their answer is the test.

steps.description: From the essential claims, find the one or two that are truly irreducible: the core of what you are.

inputs.name: essential-claims
inputs.desc: Claims that survived the subtraction test

outputs.name: irreducible-core
outputs.desc: The 1-2 claims that define what you are at the most fundamental level. Everything else is a consequence of these.

outputs.name: derivative-claims
outputs.desc: Essential claims that are true but are consequences of the core, not the core itself

process: Look at the essential claims. Ask: which of these is a cause, and which is an effect? 'Fast delivery' might be an effect of 'local production.' 'Personal service' might be an effect of 'small team by design.'
The core is the cause. The effects are derivative. You keep the derivatives in your messaging, but they orbit the core rather than competing with it.
The irreducible core is typically 1-2 statements. If you have more than 3, you have not subtracted enough. Each additional claim halves the impact of the others.
Test the core: can you explain it in one sentence to someone who knows nothing about your category? If you need two sentences, it is not yet irreducible.

steps.description: Rebuild all messaging from the irreducible core outward. The core is the headline. The derivatives are supporting points. The removed claims stay removed.

outputs.name: rebuilt-messaging
outputs.desc: New messaging framework: core statement (headline), supporting claims (subheads), and the explicit list of things you no longer say

outputs.name: channel-specific-versions
outputs.desc: The core statement adapted for each channel (website, ads, social, email, sales conversations)

process: Write the core statement as a headline. It should be one sentence. It should be specific enough that a competitor cannot copy it word for word.
Arrange the derivative claims as supporting points beneath the core. They exist to prove the core, not to compete with it.
For each channel, adapt the length but not the message. The website gets the core plus derivatives. The ad gets the core only. The sales conversation gets the core as the opening line.
Create a 'do not say' list from the removable claims. This list prevents drift back toward generic messaging.

steps.description: Set up the discipline to prevent claim creep. Without maintenance, messaging accumulates claims over time and returns to the blurry state.

outputs.name: messaging-governance-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for adding new claims: any new claim must survive the subtraction test and not contradict the core

outputs.name: quarterly-audit-checklist
outputs.desc: Checklist for re-running the subtraction exercise quarterly to catch claim creep

process: Rule: any new claim proposed for marketing materials must pass the subtraction test before it is added. If removing it would not change the right customer's decision, it does not go in.
Rule: the core statement does not change unless the business fundamentally changes. It is the anchor, not a rotating tagline.
Set a quarterly audit: re-collect all messaging, re-count the claims, and re-run the subtraction test. If the claim count has crept above the post-subtraction baseline, cut back.

description: Build content that compounds over time instead of content that decays. Compounding content answers persistent questions, ranks in search, and grows more valuable as it accumulates links and authority. One compounding piece is worth 50 decaying pieces over 3 years.

steps.description: Audit your existing content library and classify each piece as compounding or decaying based on its traffic and engagement trajectory.

inputs.name: content-library
inputs.desc: List of all published content (blog posts, articles, videos, podcasts, social posts) with publish dates

inputs.name: analytics-data
inputs.desc: Traffic, engagement, and conversion data per piece over time (at least 6 months of history)

outputs.name: content-classification
outputs.desc: Each piece classified as compounding (traffic stable or growing after 90 days) or decaying (traffic declining after 90 days)

outputs.name: compound-decay-ratio
outputs.desc: The percentage of your library that is compounding vs decaying. Most libraries are 10-20% compounding, 80-90% decaying.

process: For each piece of content, plot the traffic over time from publish date to now. If traffic is stable or growing after 90 days, it is compounding. If traffic peaked within 7 days and has been declining since, it is decaying.
Calculate the ratio. A healthy content operation has at least 30% compounding content. Below 20% means you are on a treadmill: you must constantly produce new content just to maintain traffic.
For each compounding piece, note what it has in common with other compounding pieces: topic type, format, search intent, and structure.

steps.description: Find the topics that compound: questions people will keep asking next year and the year after. These are the only topics worth investing in.

inputs.name: compound-decay-ratio
inputs.desc: Current ratio of compounding to decaying content

outputs.name: compounding-topic-list
outputs.desc: Topics that have persistent search demand (verified by search volume stability over 2+ years) and align with your expertise

outputs.name: decay-topic-avoidance-list
outputs.desc: Topic patterns to avoid or limit: news reactions, trend commentary, hot takes, and event coverage

process: Start with what already compounds in your library. What topics do those pieces cover? What format are they in? What search intent do they serve (how-to, what-is, comparison, list)?
For candidate topics, check the search volume trend over 2+ years. If the volume is stable or growing, the topic compounds. If the volume spikes and falls, it decays.
The highest-value compounding topics answer questions at the moment of decision or action: 'how to X', 'X vs Y', 'best X for Y', and 'what is X'. These serve people who are about to do something.
Create the avoidance list: news reactions, trend commentary, predictions, event recaps, and 'just announced' posts. These get a spike of traffic and then nothing. Limit them to 20% or less of output.

steps.description: Architect a compounding content piece. Compounding pieces are built differently from decaying pieces: they are comprehensive, structured for scanning, and designed to earn links.

outputs.name: content-architecture-template
outputs.desc: The structural template for a compounding piece: title formula, section structure, link-earning elements, and update triggers

outputs.name: production-standards
outputs.desc: Minimum standards for a compounding piece: depth, citations, visuals, and update commitment

process: Title formula: include the exact phrase people search for. 'How to [do X]' or '[X] vs [Y]: [difference that matters]'. The title is for search, not for cleverness.
Structure for scanning: use H2 sections that each answer a sub-question. A reader should be able to get value from any single section without reading the whole piece.
Include link-earning elements: original data, a unique framework, a comparison table, or a tool. Other sites link to things they cannot create themselves.
Plan the update cycle: compounding content must be refreshed when the information changes. Set a reminder to review and update every 6-12 months.

steps.description: Shift the production ratio toward compounding content without stopping all decaying content (which serves social and community purposes).

outputs.name: production-calendar
outputs.desc: Content calendar with explicit compounding vs decaying slots, targeting a ratio of at least 50% compounding

outputs.name: resource-reallocation
outputs.desc: How to shift production time: one compounding piece may take 5-10x the effort of a decaying piece, but delivers 50x the value over 3 years

process: Set the target ratio: at least 50% of new content production should be compounding pieces. The other 50% can be timely, social, or community content.

Reallocate effort: a compounding piece takes 5-10x longer to produce. But it delivers value for years. Budget the time accordingly: one compounding piece per week is more valuable than five decaying pieces per week.
Batch production: write the compounding pieces in focused blocks. They require research, depth, and editing. Timely pieces can be produced in the gaps.
Track the ratio monthly. If the compounding percentage drops below 40%, something is pulling production back toward the treadmill.

steps.description: Set up the refresh cycle. Compounding content decays into inaccuracy if not maintained. The refresh is what keeps it compounding.

inputs.name: content-classification
inputs.desc: Existing compounding pieces that need refresh

outputs.name: refresh-schedule
outputs.desc: Each compounding piece mapped to its refresh cadence (6 or 12 months) based on how fast the topic changes

outputs.name: refresh-checklist
outputs.desc: What to check on each refresh: factual accuracy, links still working, new information to add, outdated sections to remove, search ranking position

process: For each compounding piece, set the refresh cadence based on topic volatility. Fast-moving topics (technology, pricing): every 6 months. Stable topics (principles, processes): every 12 months.

On each refresh: check facts, update numbers, add new information that has emerged since the last version, remove anything that is no longer accurate, and re-optimize the title and structure based on current search patterns.

After each refresh, track the impact: did traffic increase? Did the piece regain or improve its search ranking? If yes, the refresh worked. If no, the topic may have shifted and the piece needs a rewrite, not a refresh.

description: Design a process where each step is a small yes that builds commitment toward a larger yes. The foot-in-the-door effect works in sales funnels, relationships, habits, and any context where you need someone to move from stranger to committed.

steps.description: Map the full journey from first contact to desired outcome. Identify the current big asks and the gaps where people drop off.

inputs.name: desired-outcome
inputs.desc: What you want the person to do (buy, join, commit, adopt, partner, hire you)

inputs.name: current-journey
inputs.desc: The current steps a person goes through from first awareness to the desired outcome

outputs.name: journey-map
outputs.desc: Each step in the current journey with the ask size (what the person must commit at that step) and the drop-off rate

outputs.name: big-ask-locations
outputs.desc: Steps where the ask jumps from small to large, creating a commitment gap that causes drop-off

process: Map every step from first contact to desired outcome. For each step, write what the person must do (click, sign up, provide info, spend time, spend money, tell someone).
Rate each ask on a scale of 1-10 where 1 is effortless (click a link) and 10 is a major commitment (sign a contract, pay thousands, change a habit permanently).
Find the gaps: where does the ask jump from a 2 to a 7 in a single step? These gaps are where people drop off. The jump is too big.
Note the current drop-off rate at each step if data is available. The highest drop-off rates will correlate with the biggest ask jumps.

steps.description: Insert small, easy commitments between the current steps to bridge the gaps. Each micro-commitment should be a natural, valuable step that happens to also increase commitment.

outputs.name: revised-journey
outputs.desc: The journey with micro-commitments inserted, where no single step increases the ask by more than 2 points

outputs.name: micro-commitment-designs
outputs.desc: For each inserted step: what the person does, what value they receive, and why it naturally leads to the next step

process: For each gap, design 1-3 intermediate steps. Each step should: (1) be genuinely valuable on its own (not busywork), (2) require slightly more commitment than the previous step, (3) provide information or experience that makes the next step feel natural.

Examples of micro-commitments: follow (low), subscribe to email (slightly higher), download a resource (higher, they gave email), attend a webinar (higher, they gave time), start a trial (higher, they changed behavior), make a small purchase (highest before the big ask).
The key: each micro-commitment must provide value independent of the next step. If a step only exists to advance the funnel, it feels manipulative and people sense it.
Redesign the journey so no single step increases the ask by more than 2 points on the 1-10 scale.

steps.description: At each micro-commitment, something accumulates that makes leaving cost more than staying. This is not about trapping people. It is about building genuine value that happens to compound.

outputs.name: accumulated-value-map
outputs.desc: At each step in the journey, what the person has built up that they would lose by leaving (knowledge, customization, relationships, progress, data)

outputs.name: natural-lock-in-points
outputs.desc: The steps where accumulated value is highest and the person would naturally choose to continue rather than start over elsewhere

process: At each step, identify what accumulates: data they have entered, preferences they have set, progress they have made, relationships they have formed, knowledge they have gained, or reputation they have built.
The accumulation must be genuine value, not artificial barriers. 'I have 6 months of data here' is genuine. 'They make it hard to export my data' is artificial and breeds resentment.

Identify the natural lock-in points: the stages where so much value has accumulated that leaving would mean starting over. These are where the big ask can be placed, because the person is already invested.

Design the big ask (the final desired outcome) to land just after a natural lock-in point. The person has already committed time, attention, and identity. The big ask feels like a natural next step, not a jump.

steps.description: Measure the funnel at every micro-commitment point. The data tells you which steps are working and which are still too big a jump.

outputs.name: measurement-framework
outputs.desc: Metrics for each step: completion rate, time between steps, and the ratio of people who reach the next step vs those who stall

outputs.name: optimization-priorities
outputs.desc: The steps with the lowest completion rates, ranked by impact on overall conversion

process: At each micro-commitment, track: how many people reach it, how many complete it, how long it takes them, and how many proceed to the next step.
Calculate the step-over-step conversion rate. If step 3 has a 90% completion rate but step 4 has a 40% completion rate, step 4 is still too big a jump.
For each low-conversion step, diagnose: is the ask too large? Is the value unclear? Is the timing wrong? Does the person have enough accumulated value to justify the ask?
Prioritize optimization by impact: improving a step where 50% of all remaining prospects drop off is more valuable than improving a step where 5% drop off.

steps.description: Calibrate the escalation rate. Too fast and people feel pushed. Too slow and they lose interest. The right pace matches the value delivery pace.

outputs.name: calibrated-funnel
outputs.desc: The final funnel with timing, pacing, and escalation calibrated based on actual data

outputs.name: funnel-documentation
outputs.desc: Complete documentation of the micro-commitment funnel: every step, its purpose, the value delivered, the commitment asked, and the measurement plan

process: Match the commitment pace to the value delivery pace. If you deliver value weekly, ask for a commitment weekly. If you deliver value daily, you can ask daily.
Test the timing between steps. Some funnels move too fast (3 emails in 3 days asking for more commitment) and some too slow (monthly touchpoints that lose momentum).
The calibration is done: when the completion rate at each step is above 50% and the time between steps matches the natural decision rhythm of your audience.
Document the final funnel. For each step: what the person does, what they receive, what accumulates, and the metrics that prove it is working.

description: Interview customers (or yourself) to discover the job they hired a product or service to do. The job, not the product category, is the competitive frame. Products that serve the same job are the real competitors, even if they are in different categories.

steps.description: Design the Jobs-to-be-Done interview. The interview follows a specific structure that uncovers the forces of progress: push, pull, anxiety, and habit.

inputs.name: product-or-service
inputs.desc: What you offer (the thing being hired for a job)

inputs.name: recent-customers
inputs.desc: A list of recent customers or users to interview (target 8-12 interviews for pattern saturation)

outputs.name: interview-guide
outputs.desc: The interview script organized by the four forces: push (situation and struggle), pull (attraction to the new solution), anxiety (what almost stopped them), and habit (what they were doing before)

outputs.name: interview-logistics
outputs.desc: Scheduling, recording consent, interview length (45-60 minutes), and compensation plan

process: Structure the interview around the timeline of the switch: first thought, passive looking, active looking, deciding, buying, first use, and ongoing use.

Key questions: What was happening in your life or work when you first thought about this? What were you using before? What was the moment you decided to make a change? What alternatives did you consider? What almost stopped you?
Do not ask about features. Ask about situations. The job lives in the situation, not in the product category.
Plan for 8-12 interviews. Patterns typically saturate (stop yielding new jobs) by interview 8. If you are still finding new jobs at interview 12, conduct 4 more.

steps.description: Conduct the interviews. The interviewer's job is to reconstruct the timeline of the decision, not to validate hypotheses.

outputs.name: interview-transcripts
outputs.desc: Full transcripts or detailed notes from each interview, organized by the timeline and forces framework

outputs.name: raw-forces-data
outputs.desc: For each interview: the push (what was wrong), the pull (what attracted them), the anxiety (what almost stopped them), and the habit (what they were doing before)

process: Start each interview by asking about the context, not the product: 'Take me back to when you first started thinking about this. What was going on?'
Follow the timeline forward. At each stage, ask 'what happened next?' and 'what were you thinking at that point?' The goal is to reconstruct the decision as a story, not as a list of criteria.
When the person mentions a feeling ('I was frustrated with...'), go deeper: 'What specifically about it frustrated you? Can you give me an example?'
Do not lead. Do not suggest. Do not validate. Your hypotheses about the job are irrelevant during the interview. The person's story is the data.

steps.description: Synthesize the interviews into job statements. A job statement follows a specific format: when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [desired outcome].

inputs.name: raw-forces-data
inputs.desc: Push, pull, anxiety, and habit for each interview

outputs.name: job-statements
outputs.desc: The 2-5 distinct jobs uncovered, each in the format: when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [desired outcome]

outputs.name: forces-diagram
outputs.desc: For each job: the four forces mapped with specific examples from the interviews

process: Group the interviews by similarity: which interviews describe the same situation and the same desired outcome? Each group is a candidate job.
For each group, write the job statement: 'When [the common situation], I want to [the common motivation], so I can [the common desired outcome].'

Test each job statement: does it explain why the person switched? Does it explain what they were switching from? Does it explain the alternatives they considered? A good job statement passes all three tests.

Map the four forces for each job: the push (dissatisfaction with the old way), the pull (attraction to the new way), the anxiety (risk of switching), and the habit (comfort of the old way). The balance of these forces determines whether someone switches.

steps.description: Redefine your competitive frame based on the job, not the product category. Your real competitors are whatever the customer would hire instead, even if it is in a completely different category.

inputs.name: job-statements
inputs.desc: The jobs your product is hired for

outputs.name: real-competitor-map
outputs.desc: For each job: the set of solutions the customer considers (including non-obvious ones from other categories, including doing nothing)

outputs.name: competitive-advantage-by-job
outputs.desc: For each job: where you win against the real competitors and where you lose

process: For each job, list every solution the interviewees mentioned considering. This includes: direct competitors, products from other categories, manual workarounds, hiring a person, and doing nothing.
'Doing nothing' is often the strongest competitor. The force of habit keeps people in the status quo even when better options exist.

For each real competitor, map where you are stronger and weaker on the four forces. You win when you reduce anxiety better, or when you have a stronger pull, or when you address the push more directly.
If a real competitor is from a completely different category, that is valuable information. It means your marketing should address the job, not the category.

steps.description: Translate the job insights into messaging. Job-based messaging speaks to the situation and the desired outcome, not to features.

inputs.name: job-statements
inputs.desc: The jobs your product is hired for

inputs.name: real-competitor-map
inputs.desc: Who you actually compete with for each job

outputs.name: job-based-messaging
outputs.desc: Messaging for each job: headline (the situation), body (how you serve the job better than the alternatives), and proof (evidence from the interviews)

outputs.name: anxiety-reducers
outputs.desc: Specific messaging elements designed to reduce the anxieties uncovered in the interviews

process: For each job, write a headline that describes the situation, not the product: 'When [situation happens], [product] gets you to [desired outcome].'

Write the body from the forces: address the push (validate the frustration), name the pull (state the benefit in the customer's own words from the interviews), and reduce the anxiety (address the specific worries they expressed).
Use the interview language directly. The words customers use to describe the job are the words other potential customers will recognize and respond to.
Do not mention features unless they directly serve the job. A feature that does not connect to the job is irrelevant in this context.

steps.description: If multiple jobs emerged, prioritize which job to serve first. Not all jobs are equally valuable or equally served by your current offering.

inputs.name: competitive-advantage-by-job
inputs.desc: Where you win for each job

outputs.name: job-priority-ranking
outputs.desc: Jobs ranked by: market size, competitive advantage, alignment with your strengths, and profitability

outputs.name: jtbd-discovery-report
outputs.desc: Complete report: the jobs, the forces, the real competitors, the messaging, and the priority ranking

process: Score each job on four dimensions: how many people have this job (market size), how well you serve it vs alternatives (competitive advantage), how well it aligns with what you are building (strategic fit), and how profitable the customers hiring for this job are.
The primary job is the one you lead with in positioning. Secondary jobs expand the market later.

Produce the final report: the jobs, the forces, the real competitors, the messaging per job, and the priority ranking. This report replaces traditional competitive analysis because it is grounded in customer behavior, not in product feature comparisons.
Plan to re-run the discovery annually or when a major product change occurs. Jobs shift as markets evolve.

description: Decompose growth into its components so you know WHERE growth is coming from or dying. Growth equals new plus resurrected minus churned. The decomposition reveals the real narrative behind the topline number.

steps.description: Prepare the cohort data: for each time period, classify every user or customer as new, retained, resurrected, or churned.

inputs.name: user-activity-data
inputs.desc: Timestamped activity or transaction data per user or customer (at least 6 months)

inputs.name: metric-definition
inputs.desc: The growth metric to decompose (active users, revenue, customers, subscribers, members, anything that grows and shrinks)

outputs.name: cohort-classification
outputs.desc: For each period: count of new (first time active), retained (active previous period and this period), resurrected (inactive last period, active this period), and churned (active last period, inactive this period)

outputs.name: growth-equation-table
outputs.desc: Period-over-period table showing: opening count + new + resurrected - churned = closing count

process: Define 'active': what constitutes activity in your context? A login, a purchase, an engagement, a payment. Be specific and consistent.

For each period (week or month), classify every user: new (first appearance ever), retained (active in both this period and the prior period), resurrected (active this period but NOT the prior period, with at least one prior period of activity), or churned (active prior period, inactive this period).
Build the equation table: for each period, Opening = prior period's active count. Closing = Opening + New + Resurrected - Churned.
Verify: the closing count must equal the actual active count for that period. If it does not, the classification logic has an error.

steps.description: Read the narrative from the numbers. The same topline growth rate can tell very different stories depending on the composition.

inputs.name: cohort-classification
inputs.desc: New, retained, resurrected, and churned counts per period

outputs.name: growth-narrative
outputs.desc: The story the data tells: is growth driven by acquisition (new), reactivation (resurrected), or retention improvement? Is churn masked by new growth?

outputs.name: health-diagnosis
outputs.desc: Assessment: healthy growth (retention improving, churn declining), leaky bucket (high new offset by high churn), or zombie growth (flat topline with different people each period)

process: If growth is positive but churn is also high: you have a leaky bucket. You are acquiring fast enough to mask attrition, but the underlying retention is weak.
If growth is positive because of resurrection: you have a reactivation story, not an acquisition story. Something brought back dormant users (a new feature, a campaign, a seasonal effect).
If retained count is growing as a percentage of active: retention is improving. This is the strongest growth signal because retained users compound.
If the active count is flat but new and churned are both high: you have zombie growth. Different people each period, no compounding. This is unsustainable.

steps.description: Build the retention curve by cohort. The shape of the curve tells you whether you have product-market fit and where you lose people.

inputs.name: growth-narrative
inputs.desc: The story the growth data tells

outputs.name: retention-curves
outputs.desc: For each acquisition cohort: the percentage still active at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 periods after joining

outputs.name: flattening-point
outputs.desc: The period at which the retention curve flattens (the natural retention rate). If it never flattens, you do not have product-market fit for that cohort.

process: For each cohort (users who joined in a given period), track what percentage are still active at each subsequent period.
Plot the curves. A healthy curve drops initially (not everyone sticks) then flattens at a stable retention rate. The flattening point and the stable rate are your two key numbers.
If the curve never flattens (it keeps declining toward zero): you do not have product-market fit for that cohort. Investigate what is different about cohorts whose curves do flatten.
Compare cohorts over time. Are newer cohorts retaining better or worse than older cohorts? Improving retention curves mean the product is getting better for new users.

steps.description: Identify which lever to pull: improve acquisition, improve retention, or reactivate dormant users. The growth accounting tells you which lever has the most impact.

outputs.name: primary-lever
outputs.desc: The single lever with the highest impact on growth: new acquisition, retention improvement, churn reduction, or reactivation

outputs.name: lever-impact-model
outputs.desc: For each lever: what a 10% improvement would produce in absolute growth terms

process: Model each lever: if you increase new by 10%, what happens to the topline? If you decrease churn by 10%? If you increase resurrection by 10%?
The lever with the highest impact per unit of effort is the priority. Usually: churn reduction has the highest impact (it compounds), followed by acquisition, then reactivation.

But the priority depends on the diagnosis: if you have a leaky bucket, fix retention first. If retention is strong but growth is slow, invest in acquisition. If you have a large dormant base, try reactivation.
Pick one lever. Trying to move all three at once diffuses effort and makes measurement impossible.

steps.description: Build the growth accounting dashboard and set the reporting cadence. This is the instrument panel for growth, not a one-time analysis.

outputs.name: dashboard-spec
outputs.desc: Dashboard layout: growth equation bar chart (new, resurrected, churned stacked per period), retention curves by cohort, and the primary lever metric with target

outputs.name: growth-accounting-report
outputs.desc: Complete growth accounting report with narrative, diagnosis, lever recommendation, and measurement plan

process: Build the dashboard with three views: (1) the growth equation stacked bar chart showing new, retained, resurrected, and churned per period, (2) retention curves by cohort, and (3) the primary lever metric tracked against the target.
Set the reporting cadence: weekly for the growth equation, monthly for the retention curves and lever metrics.
The dashboard replaces the vanity metric (topline active users or revenue) with the diagnostic metric (where growth comes from). Present this to anyone who asks 'are we growing?'

Re-run the lever analysis quarterly. The right lever changes as the business matures: early-stage companies pull acquisition. Growth-stage companies pull retention. Mature companies pull reactivation.
